messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Others Cycling: People cycling, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Mai is a 37-year-old refugee aid worker, married, living in a Midwestern city. She came to the United States from Vietnam as a child, but she returned to the region for several years with an international humanitarian organization. The trauma happened during a distribution of supplies at a camp near a border crossing. Local police arrived in force to disperse what they called an unauthorized gathering. Mai was pinned against a shipping container as officers pushed into the crowd with batons. A young man on a bicycle tried to weave through the chaos; an officer swung at him, the bicycle collapsed, and Mai watched him fall under the wheels of a police truck. She tried to reach him but another officer shoved her to the ground, his boot on her back while she screamed. She could hear the cyclist’s weeping stop. No one was held accountable. The incident was classified as a riot dispersal with minimal injuries.

In the months that followed, Mai found that she could not tolerate being in crowded spaces. The press of bodies in a supermarket aisle made her chest tighten, and she would leave her cart and walk out. She also began to notice police presence everywhere—a patrol car idling at a red light, an officer in the coffee shop—and each sighting sent a jolt of cold alertness through her. Strangely, even seeing someone cycling on a quiet residential street could undo her: the rhythm of pedals, the posture of the rider, sometimes just the soft whir of wheels. She had come to believe that any of these moments could pull her back into that day with the same visceral terror, the same grief that washed over her when the memory returned unbidden. At work, she avoided the field sites where police or crowds were likely, and she turned down invitations to team dinners or celebrations. Anything that might have made her feel happy or hopeful felt dangerous, as if permitting herself joy would leave her unprotected.

She tried not to think about what had happened. When images surfaced, she would press her palms against her eyes or start a mental list of grocery items. At night, she lay awake for hours, replaying the sound of the bicycle frame bending, the officer’s boot pressing into her spine. Her husband had begun to sleep in the guest room because her restlessness woke him. She found herself snapping at him for small things—leaving a cup on the counter, humming a tune—and she knew the anger was not about the cup, but she could not stop herself. She started gambling online, a few dollars at first, then larger sums, because the pull of the spin gave her something else to feel besides the heaviness in her chest. The losses mounted, and yet the momentary rush when the reels stopped was the only time she felt anything other than numb or terrified.

What frightened Mai most was that she no longer recognized herself. She had been someone who ran toward danger to help, who believed in order and fairness. Now she saw only injustice: what happened to her was deeply unfair, and no one had apologized, investigated, or even acknowledged it. She was certain that someone else—a different person, a stronger person—would never have gotten into that situation in the first place. That thought hollowed her out. She began to take risks that felt almost deliberate: driving through yellow lights, walking alone at night in unsafe neighborhoods, as if daring the world to finish what the police had started.

Last month, Mai’s husband found the credit card statement. He did not yell; he simply said he could not live this way anymore. That night, she stayed on the bathroom floor, rocking, the memory so vivid that she could smell diesel and dust, could hear the cyclist’s last exhale. She knew she could not stop the memory, the grief, the rage, the gambling, on her own. She called the employee assistance program the next morning. She is hoping that someone can help her stop the spiral, but she is afraid that talking about it will only make the memories more real—and that she will finally have to admit that the person she used to be is gone.
